title: The Wild Ox and the Unicorn
lead: The Hebrew re'em is a strong wild animal with horns. It is named in nine verses of the Old Testament, almost always as a picture of power. Modern translations call it the wild ox. It was probably the aurochs, the huge wild cattle that are now extinct. The Greek Septuagint called it monokeros, "one-horn." The Latin Vulgate made it a rhinoceros in some verses and a unicorn in others. The King James Version has "unicorn" in all nine. It is a classic case of a guess handed down from one translation to the next.

sections.b: The re'em usually stands for strength that no one can tame. Balaam says twice of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, "he has the horns of a wild ox" (Numbers 23:22; Numbers 24:8). Moses blesses Joseph: "his horns are a wild ox's horns" (Deuteronomy 33:17). God asks Job, "Can you rope the wild ox to plow a furrow?" (Job 39:10). It looks like the farmer's ox, but it will never work for him. The psalmist gives thanks: "But you have lifted my horn like a wild ox's" (Psalm 92:10). In Psalm 29:6 the LORD sets Lebanon jumping "like a calf," and Sirion "like a wild ox's young." Twice the animal is not a picture of good strength. In Psalm 22:21 the wild oxen are among the psalmist's enemies: "From the horns of the wild oxen you have answered me." In Isaiah's judgment on Edom the wild oxen go down with the bulls in a great slaughter (Isaiah 34:6–7).

sections.h: How the wild ox became a unicorn
sections.b: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus. In Swete's edition it renders re'em as monokeros, "one-horned," in Numbers 23:22 and 24:8, Deuteronomy 33:17, Job 39:9 and the Psalms. It even puts a unicorn into Psalm 78:69. There the Hebrew has ramim, "heights," and Psalm 22:21 spells the animal's name with the same letters (remim). In Isaiah 34:7 the Greek has "the stout ones" instead. The Latin Vulgate has "rhinoceros" in Numbers 23:22, Deuteronomy 33:17 and Job 39:9–10. It has "unicorn" in Psalm 22:21 and Isaiah 34:7. The King James Version (1611) has "unicorn" or "unicorns" in all nine verses. Later English versions changed course. The American Standard Version (1901) has "wild-ox." Young's Literal Translation keeps the Hebrew name, "reem." Modern versions such as the BSB and WEB have "wild ox."

sections.b: The Hebrew answers the question. In Deuteronomy 33:17 Joseph's horns are qarne re'em, "the horns of a wild ox." The word for horns is in the Hebrew dual, the form used for a pair. So one animal has two horns. Psalm 29:6 sets the animal beside the calf, and Job 39:9–12 sets it beside the plow ox, so it is a kind of cattle. The STEPBible lexicon gives "wild ox," "probably the great aurochs or wild bulls which are now extinct." It adds that the exact meaning is not known. Tertullian also turned away from the one-horned beast, but he did not argue from the Hebrew. He argued from the cross: Moses' blessing, he wrote, points to "no one-horned rhinoceros" and no "two-horned minotaur," but to Christ, whose horns are the ends of the cross (An Answer to the Jews 10).

Early Christians read these horns as pictures of the cross. Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, said that "the horns of an unicorn" in Moses' blessing of Joseph portray the cross. The upright beam rises like one horn, and the ends of the crossbeam stand out like horns on either side (Dialogue with Trypho 91). Tertullian (about AD 200) made the same point. He added Psalm 22:21, the psalm Christians read as Jesus' suffering: "from the horn of the unicorns" meant the ends of the cross (An Answer to the Jews 10). The picture works just as well with the wild ox's pair of horns. In the Hebrew the wild ox usually means strength, whether God's or the beast's own. In two verses it is an enemy or a victim (Psalm 22:21; Isaiah 34:7).
